content.title: Artemis II Launch: What to know about NASA’s First Crewed Moon Flyby Since the 1970s - Futura-Sciences
content.text: Some say this launch is an important milestone on the path to pushing humanity to deep space, bringing new space riches to Earth’s peoples, and opening the door to interplanetary colonisation. “I think it’s going to be fascinating,” said Dr. Kyler Kuehn, acting director of science at the Lowell Observatory in Arizona, USA. Others scoff at the launch’s unremarkable nature and the commercial entanglements that could hinder Artemis’s progress. Discover moreSciencessciencesscientific Here’s what you need to know to catch up ahead of the upcoming launch. On the day, you can watch the launch live here. NASA will provide free, commented coverage of the launch on the day. We will update this post with a live feed for the event. In the meantime, you can enjoy a live feed of the rocket here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xCrPD7tfcr0 Artemis 2 will go around the Moon Artemis will be the first human lunar flyby in over 50 years. The main goal of Artemis 2 is to test whether the equipment NASA has developed is fit for purpose, since it’s been a while since humans have gone to the Moon. “This is something that we did six decades ago, but all the engineers who did that are long gone,” said Kuehn. The ten-day flight will bring humans around the far side of the Moon before returning to Earth. During that time, engineers and crew members will test the launch system, the crew’s living quarters, communication between Earth and the Moon-bound crew, and the crew’s ability to pilot the spaceship, among other things. This is step 2 of a decade-long program that aims to bring humans back to the Moon, and beyond Artemis 2 is only the second stage of a long-reaching mission to put humans on the Moon, a feat not achieved since 1972. “President Kennedy and early NASA were a bit ahead of their time, accomplishing some amazing things. Now, we need to be able to do this sort of thing consistently,” said Kuehn. Unlike the Apollo missions of the 60s and 70s, the ambition is not only to go to the Moon, but to lay the building blocks for going there more often. Artemis will also aim to build the lunar Gateway, a small space station assembled in orbit around the Moon that will serve as an outpost for astronauts exploring the lunar surface. These plans are only a “stepping stone” on the way to grander aspirations, Kuehn reported. The ultimate goal is for humanity to become a “multi-planet” species, able to mine asteroids, put data centers in space, and go to Mars, for instance, he said. “We’ve had the space station as a presence in space, and astronauts there continuously for decades now. But there’s more than just being in space. There’s utilizing it,” he said. Mission Objectives Status/Target Date Artemis I Uncrewed SLS/Orion lunar orbit test Completed Nov 16, 2022 ​ Artemis II First crewed Orion lunar flyby As early as April 2026 Artemis III First crewed lunar landing since 1972, near the lunar South Pole. Orion will rendezvous with a lunar lander in orbit (SpaceX Starship or other), which will bring astronauts to the lunar surface. Unknown, one source suggests 2028 at the earliest, though this is unconfirmed by NASA Artemis IV, V, VI The Gateway core is delivered to lunar orbit and gets gradually more elaborate with each mission. 2nd, 3rd, and 4th landings on the Moon. Unknown Artemis X+ Long-term lunar stays (up to 180 days); Mars tech demos 2035+ Artemis 2 is due to bring the first woman and the first person of color on board a lunar mission @ https://www.nasa.gov/artemis-ii-media-resources/ The crew is made up of NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, and Canadian Space Agency’s Jeremy Hansen. On top of their many professional achievements, Koch and Glover will be able to say they were the first woman and first person of color on a lunar mission. The spaceship will be launched by one of the most powerful rockets ever built @https://www.nasa.gov/image-detail/amf-ksc-20260128-ph-csh01-0009/ NASA’s Space Launch System (SLS) is one of the biggest rockets ever built for spaceflight. When fully stacked up with its Orion spacecraft and launch abort system (see below), it measures about 322 feet / 98 meters tall, which is only surpassed by SpaceX’s Starship. That’s taller than the Statue of Liberty from base to torch, or the tower that carries Big Ben in London. It has flown only once before, during NASA’s Artemis I mission in November 2022. On its second launch, it will boost the crew through the Earth’s atmosphere using more than 8.8 million pounds of thrust. SLS will only be used for 8 minutes of the 10-day journey While the SLS is capturing the public’s imagination, it is only really used for is brute force at the very start of the journey. For most of the mission, the crew will be inside the Orion spacecraft, a much smaller pod that stands at 67 ft/20.4 m when fully stacked with its launch abort system (see below), and 26 ft/7.9 m when the launch abort system is discarded. The Orion spacecraft’s crew module, the pressurized part of the spacecraft where the crew works and lives during the journey, is fairly cramped, with only 330 ft 3 / 9.34 m3 of habitable volume for the 10-day journey. If there’s a problem during launch, the launch abort system will kick in or the launch duration only, the Orion spacecraft will be topped by a launch abort system (LAS), a module with its own motors that can activate within milliseconds of an adverse event to detach and bring the astronauts back to safety. In the event of a successful launch, the LAS jettisons from Orion to allow it to continue on its journey. These are the big moments to look out for during the flight Day one, day two, day six, and day ten are when you’ll want to tune in. Flight Day Key Events Day one First ten minutes: The SLS launcher pushes the spacecraft into space, detaches, and then falls back to Earth. Next 23 hours: Orion gears up to head to the Moon. Orion continues its journey, pushed forward first by the rocket’s “upper stage”, called the Interim Cryogenic Propulsion Stage (ICPS), then separating from the ICPS. The crew takes over the controls of Orion and simulates a docking situation using the ICPS as a dummy target. Day two Translunar Injection: The crew wakes up to the prospect of heading to the Moon. In the last big engine fire of the mission, Orion boosts forward using its own engines to head towards the Moon. The “translunar injection” is a big “go, no go” moment for the mission, said Kuehn. Once they are on track, the spacecraft will fly to the Moon until just before they go to bed on the fifth day. Day six The rocket will go into a loop around the Moon, exposing the far side to human eyes for the first time in over 50 years. Depending on when they launch and how far the Moon is from Earth at that time, the spacecraft will pass between 4,000 and 6,000 miles above the lunar surface. During a 30-minute window, Earth will lose communication with the spacecraft. Astronauts will then take photos and videos of the Moon. The spaceship continues on its trajectory, heading back to Earth. Day 10 Splashdown in the Pacific Ocean The crew will be monitoring their health… at a time when the sun is more likely to spew dangerous particles Part of the mission will be medical monitoring of the crew in space. This is crucial information as scientists are still figuring out what space travel does to the human body, and if humans are to go deeper into space, for longer flights, that’s information we need to know. This mission also takes place just after a solar maximum, a period when the sun is more active. The sun is constantly hurling solar particles, and usually they don’t cause much harm to humans since the Earth’s magnetic shield protects surface dwellers by bouncing most of the particles away. However, space travellers are much more exposed, and it’s important to understand the health risks of exposure and how to mitigate them. “That’s something that’s a very big concern that we’re going to need to figure out — What is the effect, even for a short-duration flight, on the crew?” said Kuehn. The crew will be testing a radiation shelter during flight Thankfully, the crew is not completely helpless in the face of solar radiation. During the Artemis I mission, NASA tested exposure to space radiation using two humanoid dummies, nicknamed Helga and Zoltar. @https://www.nasa.gov/missions/artemis/artemis-1/artemis-i-radiation-measurements-validate-orion-safety-for-astronauts/ Using this approach, they identified nooks and crannies in the Orion spacecraft that provided four times more radiation protection than other parts of the capsule. Tipping the spacecraft also provided more cover against exposure. Per NASA’s mission description, the crew will test this radiation shelter during this spaceflight. The launch has been delayed a few times during “wet dress” rehearsals The original flight window for Artemis 2 was early February, but technical issues were uncovered during the first two “wet dress” rehearsals, a pre-launch test during which the rocket is fueled on its launch pad to identify and resolve issues before launch. After the last wet dress rehearsal on February 19, the team identified an issue with the flow of pressurised helium in the rocket, which needed to be addressed. The next launch window is now set for early April. Expect this flight to be “technically unremarkable” — which would be “remarkable” in its own way, experts comment While the Artemis 2 mission marks a landmark in humans’ return to the Moon, it’s likely to be “technically unremarkable,” said Dr Bleddyn Bowen, associate professor in astropolitics at Durham University, UK, adding that Artemis 2 is “just the same” as Artemis 1, “but with people in it.” “It’s doing stuff the Americans did decades ago,” he said. For Kuehn, however, even achieving an unremarkable flight will be remarkable. “This is a new spacecraft, so a lot of it’s basically just learning how to [go to the Moon] again,” said Kuehn. He also notes that allowing the crew to operate the machinery should provide significant insight for ground-based teams. “Learning how to maneuver the spacecraft effectively is an important, I think it’s also one of the important technical milestones,” he said. Artemis 3 will be the real test of NASA’s program, said Bowen For Bowen, the program will still have a lot to prove, even if Artemis II is successful. “The interesting bit is what happens after Artemis II,” he said. Critics have raised concerns about the program’s inflated budget and delayed timelines, with the SLS’s per-launch cost estimated at roughly $2 billion. According to Reuters, Artemis is under increased internal pressure to accelerate its progress. From Artemis III, NASA will be expected to put boots on the Moon. At first, this will be achieved by astronauts meeting with another spacecraft near the Moon that will bring them down to the surface of the Moon. This spacecraft, called a lunar lander, is being developed by a commercial partner. Until recently, SpaceX was the firm set to act as this lunar shuttle, having won the contract in 2021. But the firm’s development has been met with frequent explosions during its Starship launcher’s test launches, and reported planned delays to fueling demonstrations, reusability, and uncrewed lunar landing demonstrations. “There are no landers, there are no spacesuits — you sort of need those if you’re going to go to the Moon,” Bowen said. Congress is now “seemingly displeased with the apparent lack of progress with Starship,” Bowen said. Indeed, the body reopened the lunar lander contract up to competition in late 2025, leaving a gap open for Blue Origin to compete for the lunar lander spot. Per Bowen, “the great irony, of course, is that for years, many people have been criticizing NASA and the public sector as being slow and wasteful and non-innovative. But it’s only NASA that’s actually got the working stuff to get anywhere near [the Moon] right now.”
